new_statements.rule_in_words: Mawng has no lexical tone and is (implicitly, after Capell & Hinch) a stress-accent/intonational language. Preliminary generalisations from a six-speaker Warruwi corpus: mono- and disyllables always initial stress; a heavy non-initial syllable (e.g. murlirrk) does not attract stress, so the system is taken to be quantity-insensitive with leftmost (trochaic) stress; in nouns the accent almost always falls on the leftmost foot (first syllable of the root); trisyllables carry stress on the first or second syllable, variably within and across speakers; words of four or more syllables carry two stresses, initial and penultimate (of word or root), and which one is primary varies from word to word. For their alignment study the authors 'assume initial stress assignment in Mawng'. Footnote 7 (p. 6) explicitly notes that Capell & Hinch (1970:27) 'suggest that stress assignment is quantity sensitive (being attracted to a heavy antepenult) in words of four or more syllables; their account is however very brief and does not take morphological structure into account.' They also adopt the working hypothesis that F0 is the most consistent correlate of word stress, and (sec. 3.4, p. 19) cannot exclude an alternative in which the F0 rise on every prosodic word is a word-initial phrase tone (LHw) anchored at the left edge rather than a pitch accent on the stressed syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Words of four or more syllables 'tend to have two stresses, on both initial and penultimate syllables (of the word or root)', primary vs secondary status undetermined (p. 7); occasional words bear two pitch accents and the authors 'leave open.. whether these additional stresses should be considered as instances of primary stress.. or as an instance of rhythmic secondary stress' (pp. 10-11).
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllabic words vary between first- and second-syllable stress within one speaker and across speakers, including the loan name 'Amanda' (p. 7), which the authors tie to Capell & Hinch's 'first two syllables.. tend to be equally stressed'; verbs with heavy prefixes have stress that is harder to locate and more variable than nominals (p. 5); F0 and intensity peaks often fall on different syllables within the first two syllables (pp. 6-7); non-clitic function words are usually unaccented (p. 10).
new_statements.identity_note: All HKS 2007 data were recorded at Warruwi (Goulburn Island), six speakers; the language is Mawng = Maung (maun1240), no dialect distinction drawn. Comparisons in the paper to Iwaidja (Birch 2002) and Bininj Gun-wok (Bishop 2003) are about other languages and were not used for the Mawng reading.

readall_conflicts: Hellmuth, Kuegler & Singer 2007 (the only listed work, now opened from a CORE copy) analyse Mawng word stress as leftmost/initial, trochaic and quantity-insensitive (mono/disyllables always initial; trisyllables 1st or 2nd, variable; 4+ syllables initial AND penultimate with the primary varying word to word; working assumption 'initial stress assignment'). Capell & Hinch 1970 sec. 1.4 (p. 27, recovered in this our files from publisher snippets, not a listed work here) instead say stress is non-contrastive, the first two syllables of words up to three syllables are equally stressed, words of four or more syllables have penultimate stress with additional stresses on alternate preceding syllables, and a closed (CVC, CVCC) syllable before the penult tends to take the primary stress; HKS footnote 7 explicitly rejects that quantity-sensitivity claim as brief and morphology-blind. Fletcher et al. 2015 (ICPhS, held by the project from an earlier reading) give no rule but transcribe non-initial stresses (/ŋaˈɳampala/, /iˈmaʈuk/, /kataˈpaŋa/) that sit better with C&H's penult/heavy-antepenult account than with HKS's initial default. So the sources disagree on which of the two prominences (initial vs penultimate) is primary in longer words and on weight-sensitivity, while agreeing that stress is non-lexical and that short words are indeterminate between first and second syllable.

sources.quote: 'It is traditionally described as a stress language and our earlier studies [7] suggest that the prosodic typology of Mawng ... is best characterized as a head/edge prominence language with major prominence-lending pitch movements docked to a word accent that denote the left edge of an accentual phrase and right-edge tones that often delimit the edge of a phonological word.' No word-stress placement rule; no weight statement.
